## Methods

Ethics statement
All animal experiments were conducted in compliance with the guidelines outlined in the Guide
for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. All animal studies were conducted according to
protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care Committee of Nankai University (Tianjin,
China) and were performed under protocol no. IACUC 2020030501.

Bacterial strains, primers, plasmids and growth conditions
Bacterial strains, plasmids and primers used in this study are provided in Supplementary Table 1
and 2. C. sakazakii strain ATCC 29544 spontaneously developed resistance to nalidixic acid was
used as the wild-type (WT) strain throughout this study. Mutant strains of C. sakazakii were
generated using the -red recombination system by pKD3 or pKD4 plasmid with
chloramphenicol or kanamycin resistance genes 58. A helper plasmid named pCP20 encoding the
FLP recombinases was used to eliminate the antibiotic resistance gene, when required.
Complementary plasmids were constructed using pACYC184, and electroporated into
corresponding mutant strains. For purification of ArcA-6×His, arcA was fused with pET28a
expression vector and transferred into E. coli BL21 (DE3). To generate the frr-lux reporter
fusion, the amplification products of frr promoter region was digested and cloned into the Xho I–
BamH I site of the plasmid pMS402, which carries a promoterless luxCDABE reporter gene
cluster. For ChIP DNA purification, arcA was tagged with 3×Flag, and fused with pTRC99A and
electroporated into C. sakazakii ATCC 29544. All the strains constructed in the study were
verified by sequencing. Bacteria were inoculated into fresh Luria-Bertani (LB) or M9 minimal
medium (1×M9 salts, 2 mM MgSO4, 0.1 mM CaCl2, 0.4% glucose) and grown at 37 ºC under
aerobic (250 rpm) or anaerobic (90 % N2, 5 % CO2, 5 % H2; Sheldon Manufacturing) conditions.
When needed, isopropyl β-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG) and antibiotics were added to the medium
at the following final concentrations: 0.1 mM IPTG, 50 μg/ml nalidixic acid, 25 μg/ml
chloramphenicol (Cm), 50 μg/ml kanamycin (Kan), and 10 μg/ml tetracycline (TE).

Northern blot analysis
Total RNA (5-10 µg) was normalized and samples were mixed with 2 × RNA loading buffer
(Beyotime, China). RNA was separated on 6% acrylamide gels containing 8 M urea after heating
65 ºC for 15 min. Bands were transferred to nylon membranes and crosslinked by UV.
Biotinylated oligonucleotides were used as probes and hybridizations performed in the
BeyoHyb™ Quick Hybridization Solution (Beyotime, China) at 42 ºC overnight. The
membranes were washed twice with low stringency wash solution at room temperature for 5 min
each time, and washed once at 42 ºC for 2 min. The subsequences were subjected to the Biotin
Northern Blot Kit (for Small RNA) Kit (Beyotime, China). Northern blots were visualized using
Amersham Imager 600, 5S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) was used as an internal control.

Race assays
Simultaneous determination of 5′ and 3′ ends of sRNA was performed using rapid amplification
of complementary DNA ends (RACE) kits (Invitrogen, USA) essentially as manufacturer’s
instructions. The oligonucleotides used for RACE are listed in Supplementary Table 2. In each
case, the generated PCR products by specific reverse primer of correct size were directly cloned
into the pEASY-T1 vector (TransGen, China). Plasmids with sRNA RACE inserts were
sequenced using M13 forward and reverse oligonucleotides.

Cell culture and C. sakazakii infection of macrophages
Murine macrophage cell line RAW264.7 (ATCC TIB-71) was obtained from the Shanghai
Institute of Biochemistry and cultured in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS
(Hyclone, USA) at 37 °C under a 5% CO2 atmosphere.
RAW264.7 cells were infected with WT or the indicated mutant or complemented strains that
grown to the logarithmic phase at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 100. The cell monolayers
were incubated for 45 minutes following infection, rinsed three times in PBS, and incubated for
another 1 hour in RPMI 1640 media containing gentamicin (100 μg/ml) to kill the extracellular
bacteria. Then each well containing bacterial cells were rinsed three times in PBS and
replenished with RPMI 1640 containing gentamicin (10 μg/ml) supplemented with 1 mM NaNO3
when required and incubated at 37 ºC with 5% CO2. From this point, the hour post-infection
(hpi) was deemed as 0. At 1, 4 and 24 hpi, the infected cells were washed three times with PBS
and lysed with 0.05% Triton X-100 (Solarbio, China). The intracellular bacteria were enumerated
on LB agar plates for CFU analysis or collected for qRT-PCR analysis. The fold intracellular
replication of the indicated strains was expressed as the CFUs recovered at 4 or 24 hpi relative to
those at 1 hpi.

RNA isolation and Quantitative RT–PCR (qRT–PCR)
Overnight culture of C. sakazakii WT strain and mutant strains were 1:100 subcultured in 20 ml
fresh LB medium at 37 ºC with shaking at 180 rpm until the exponential growth phase was
reached (OD600 = 0.6-0.8). For C. sakazakii collected from the cells, RAW264.7 cells were
infected by C. sakazakii WT or mutant strains at a MOI of 100:1 and collected at 1, 4 and 24 hpi.
For C. sakazakii collected from the small intestine and colon, 2- to 5-day-old Sprague-Dawley
rat pups were orally infected by 1 × 108 CFU of C. sakazakii WT or mutant strains, and collected
following the contents were removed at 48 hpi. For C. sakazakii treated with rifampicin, C.
sakazakii WT strain and mutant strains were incubated with 100 μg/ml of rifampicin and
collected at 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 min. For the effect of oxygen levels on C. sakazakii, mid-
logarithmic phase C. sakazakii WT or mutant strains incubated in LB medium were collected and
reincubated in M9 minimal medium supplemented under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions
for 30 minutes.
Total RNA was extracted and purified using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA). RNA was treated
with DNase I at 37℃ for 30 min and successful removal of DNA contamination was verified by
PCR. Then the RNA was quantified and qualified by measuring the A260/A280 absorbance ratio
using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher, USA).
cDNA synthesis was performed by StarScript III RT MasterMix (GenStar, China). qRT-PCR was
performed using 2×RealStar TPower SYBR qPCR Mix (Low ROX) (GenStar, China) on
QuantStudio 5 (Applied Biosystems, USA). The expression levels of C. sakazakii transcripts
were normalized to that of the rpoA gene 59, whereas those of the small intestine and colon
transcripts were normalized to GAPDH expression. The fold change in the expression of each
target gene was estimated using the 2−ΔΔCt method.

RNA sequencing
Overnight-cultured bacteria of C. sakazakii WT and CsrN strains were inoculated into fresh LB
medium with a ratio of 1:100 further cultured till the OD600 value reached approximately 0.6, and
then collected by centrifugation for RNA extraction with three biological replicates per sample.
The RNA quality was assessed with an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Santa Clara, CA) and agarose
gel electrophoresis (AGE). Illumina library preparation, sequencing, and data analysis were
conducted by Novogene (Bejing, China). Sequenced reads were checked for base quality,
trimmed where 50% of the bases were below quality score 20, and filtered to exclude adapters.
The clean reads were mapped to the C. sakazakii strain ATCC 29544 reference genome
(CP011047.1) by using the short-sequence alignment software Bowtie 2. Gene expression levels
were normalized and reported as FPKM. For differentially expressed genes (DEGs) analysis, raw
read counts were normalized by TMM method and DEGs was performed using the edgeR
package with a significance threshold of |log2(fold change)| > 1 and false discovery rate (FDR)-
adjusted p-values < 0.005 (Benjamini-Hochberg correction).

Growth assays
For aerobic growth, overnight cultures were diluted 1:1,000 into fresh LB, RPMI 1640 medium
or M9 minimal medium. When indicated, the media were supplemented with 40 mM nitrate, 0.5
mM tungstate, or 1 mM molybdate. 200 l aliquot was added to a 96 well microplate and
incubated at 37 °C at 180 rpm for 24 h aerobically. The optical density at 600 nm was measured
every 20 min. The experiment was performed in triplicate for each strain. For anaerobic growth,
cultures under exponential growth phase (OD600 = 0.6) at a final concentration of 1 × 108
CFU/ml, supplemented as follows: (1) 40 mM NaNO₃; (2) 0.5 mM tungstate; (3) 1 mM
molybdate; (4) 40 mM NaNO₃ and 0.5 mM tungstate; and (5) 40 mM NaNO₃ with both tungstate
and molybdate at the following molar ratios, 1:2, 10:1, and 100:1, and incubated under anaerobic
(90 % N2, 5 % CO2, 5 % H2; Sheldon Manufacturing) 60 growth conditions at 37 ºC. The bacteria
suspension was diluted with PBS and spread on agar plates for enumeration of bacterial CFUs at
1, 4 and 24 hours, respectively.

Protein expression, purification and electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs)
The constructed pET28a-ArcA plasmid was transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3). pET-ArcA-
containing strain was cultured overnight in LB and 1:100 subcultured in fresh LB to OD600 = 0.6-
0.8 at 37 °C. Then IPTG was added to induce the expression of ArcA and growth at 16 °C for 20
h. The bacteria were lysed by using sonication and centrifuged at 4 °C (12,000 × g, 30 min). The
supernatant containing ArcA was subsequently purified using HiTrap Ni2+-chelating column.
Protein concentration was determined according to the Bradford method 61.
CsrN fragments of the promotor regions and point mutant were amplified by PCR and purified
using StarPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit (GenStar, China), as well as the DNA fragments of kana
DNA (negative control). The DNA fragment (40 ng) was incubated at 37 °C for 40 min with
different concentrations of 6× His-tagged ArcA protein (0-1.75 M) in 20 l binding buffer (100
mM Tris-HCl [pH 7.4], 100 mM KCl, 10mM MgCl, 10% glycerol, and 2 mM dithiothreitol).
When needed, 30 mM acetyl phosphate was added to the binding system. Samples were then
separated on 6% polyacrylamide gel in 0.5 × Tris-Borate-EDTA (TBE) for electrophoresis. DNA
fragments were stained with GelRed (Life-iLab, China).

mRNA stability assay
Overnight culture of C. sakazakii WT strain and mutant strains were 1:100 subcultured in 20 ml
fresh LB medium at 37 ºC with shaking at 180 rpm until the exponential growth phase was
reached (OD600 = 0.6). The medium was then centrifuged and the bacteria were re-suspended
with M9, to which rifampicin (100 μg/ml) was added. At each indicated time point after
rifampicin treatment, the same volume of bacteria was collected, and the corresponding RNA
was extracted immediately for qRT-PCR.

REMSAs
The target DNA templates were transcribed into CsrN, CsrN+ (positive control), CsrNmut sRNA,
5′ UTR-narGHJI, 5′ UTR-narGHJImut mRNA using T7 High Efficiency Transcription Kit
(TransGen, China) and purified by MagicPure® RNA Beads (TransGen, China). REMSA was
performed with CsrN, CsrNmut sRNA (0, 10, 20 and 30 μM) and 5′ UTR-narGHJI, 5′ UTR-
narGHJImut mRNA or CsrN+ (10 μM) in REMSA binding buffer (10 mM HEPES [pH 7.3], 20
mM KCl, 2.4 mM MgCl2, and 2.4 mM DTT). The reaction mixtures were incubated for 3 min at
85 ºC and then at 37 ºC for 45 min. RNA was separated by 6% native polyacrylamide gel
electrophoresis (PAGE) using a Native-PAGE Preparation kit (Sangon, China) and stained with
GelRed (Life-iLab, China) for 10 min, and imaged using a gel imaging system (Tanon).

DNA affinity pull-down assay
DNA pull-down assays were conducted as previously described 62, with modifications to
optimize protein-DNA interaction capture. A biotin-labeled DNA fragment encompassing the
CsrN promoter region was PCR-amplified from C. sakazakii and immobilized on streptavidin-
coated Dynabeads (Invitrogen, USA). The DNA-bound beads were incubated with crude protein
extracts from C. sakazakii wild-type strains under optimized binding conditions. Following
rigorous washing to remove nonspecifically bound proteins, the retained proteins were eluted
using a high-salt buffer (500 mM NaCl), resolved by SDS-PAGE, and visualized through
Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining. Protein bands of interest were excised from the gel, subjected
to in-gel tryptic digestion, and analyzed by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time-of-
flight tandem mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS/MS). Peptide sequences and mass spectra
were compared against the NCBI non-redundant database for protein identification.

Animal model
2- to 5-day-old Sprague-Dawley rats were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory
Animal Technology Co., Ltd. (licensed by Charles River), and housed in specific-pathogen-free
(SPF) mouse facilities. For colonization experiments, rats were infected orally with 108 CFU of
C. sakazakii WT strain and mutant strains in the logarithmic phase of growth 63. 48 hours later,
blood specimens were collected for bacterial cultures (CFU). Small intestine and colon were
collected and the contents were removed. Liver, spleen small intestine and colon were weighed
and homogenized with PBS, and spread on agar plates for enumeration of bacterial CFUs. For
survival assays, 2- to 5-day-old Sprague-Dawley rat pups were infected orally with 107 CFU of
C. sakazakii WT strain and mutant strains in the logarithmic phase of growth 64. The numbers of
animals alive was recorded every 8 hours.

In vivo bioluminescence imaging (BLI)
The DNA fragment of frr promotor were amplified, purified, and digested with BamH I/Xho I.
The products were ligated to pMS402 plasmid to construct of lux fusion plasmids 23, which was
introduced into C. sakazakii WT, CsrN, narGHJI and CsrNnarGHJI strains, respectively.
The plasmids and insertions were verified by Sanger sequencing. 2- to 5-day-old Sprague-
Dawley rats were infected by oral gavage with the strains harboring lux fusions (108 CFU). At 48
hours, rats were imaged and followed by in vivo BLI using the in vivo imaging system Lumina II
(Caliper Life Sciences, USA). Data acquisition and analysis were performed using living image
software (Caliper Life Sciences, USA).

Lux reporter assay
For lux reporter fusion, the 5′ UTR or 5′ UTRmut of narGHJI were cloned into the pMS402
plasmid through BamH I/Xho I, respectively. For sRNA overexpression plasmids, the DNA
fragments of CsrN and CsrNmut were cloned into the pNM12 plasmid through Msc I/EcoR I,
respectively. The empty pNM12 vector was labeled as control. The lux reporters and sRNA
overexpression plasmids were then transformed into CsrN strain. The plasmids and insertions
were verified by Sanger sequencing. The expression of lux-based reporters from CsrN strains
growing in liquid culture with 0.1% arabinose (inducing the expression of sRNA) was measured
using the Spark multimode microplate reader (Tecan, Switzerland).

Measurement of nitrate and nitrite concentration
The small intestine and colon of normal rat pups or that infected with C. sakazakii WT were
collected, removed the contents and homogenized in PBS containing protease inhibitors of
choice, then centrifuge at 10,000 × g for 20 minutes at 4 ºC. Transfer the supernatant to another
tube as tissue samples. The cell supernatant of RAW264.7 infected with C. sakazakii WT at 1, 4
and 24 hpi, respectively, and uninfected cell supernatant were collected as cell samples. The
following procedures were carried out according to the specification of Nitrate/Nitrite
Colorimetric Assay Kit (Cayman, USA). Firstly, to determination concentration of total nitrate
and nitrite, 80 l samples were added to 96-wells, then 10 l nitrate reductase cofactors
preparation and 10 l nitrate reductase enzyme preparation was added. After incubation for 2-3
hours, 50 µl of Griess reagent 1 and Griess reagent 2 was added, and absorbance was measured
at 540nm about 10 minutes later. Secondly, to determination concentration of nitrite, 100 l
samples were added to 96-wells, then 50 µl of Griess reagent 1 and Griess reagent 2 was added,
and absorbance was measured at 540nm about 10 minutes later. The nitrate concentration is
equal to the total nitrate and nitrite concentration calculated using the nitrate standard curve
minus the nitrite concentration calculated using the nitrite standard curve.

Cytotoxicity Assay
A lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release assay was performed to assess cytotoxicity during
bacterial infection. Following the infection of RAW264.7 cells with C. sakazakii WT, the
indicated mutant or complemented strain, culture supernatants were collected at 1, 4 and 24 hpi.
The supernatants from uninfected cells were used as a negative control. Cytotoxicity was
quantified using the Cytotox 96 non-radioactive cytotoxicity assay (Promega), and the
percentage of cytotoxicity was calculated according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

16S rRNA gene sequencing and analysis
Caecal content samples were collected from 2- to 5-day-old rat pups, which were allocated into
an untreated control group (Mock) and a tungstate-treated group (Tungstate; 48 hours of
treatment), with 8 animals per group, and extracted the total DNA. The V3-V4 hypervariable
region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene was amplified by PCR using the primer pair 338F (5’-
ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCA-3’) and 806R (5’-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3’). The
resulting PCR products were purified, and sequencing libraries were constructed. Paired-end
sequencing was subsequently performed on a NextSeq 2000 system (Illumina, USA). All the
analysis was carried out on the Majorbio platform on the website at https://cloud.majorbio.com.
α-diversity were calculated by software of Mothur (http://www.mothur.org/wiki/Calculators,
version v1.30.2), and Principal Co-ordinates Analysis (PCoA) were conducted for the analysis of
β-diversity. The comparisons among the microbiota compositions on the genus level were
conducted using Vegan v2.5-3 package.

Statistics
For each experiment, the number of independent replicates is indicated in the figure legends,
along with the corresponding statistical test used. Statistical significance was analyzed with
GraphPad Prism 9.5.0 software (GraphPad Inc). Data were analyzed with either a Student’s t-test
to compare two conditions with normal distributions or a Mann–Whitney U-test for two
conditions without normal distributions. For assessing statistical significance among three or
more groups, a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), two-way ANOVA or Dunnett’s test were
utilized as indicated. Survival analysis was used log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. Differences were
considered significant at p < 0.05.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The authors describe the characterization of a novel sRNA that regulates the nar operon and allows C. sakazakii to metabolize nitrate under anaerobic conditions. Moreover, they provide evidence that tungsten supplementation can suppress C. sakazakii infection in an animal model, as has been previously shown for Enterobacteriaceae sp. C. sakazakii has been implicated in infections of infants, often associated with contaminated formula. This is a timely report with a logical flow of experiments from initial regulator discovery to functional consequence to validation in an animal model. However, there are numerous issues that are currently unclear in the current manuscript as detailed below:
1. The RNA sequencing section is woefully incomplete. There is no details of how many samples were sequenced, their growth conditions, how the sequencing was done quality controlled or mapped to the reference strain. Were the authors able to confirm deletion of the csrN transcript in their RNA seq dataset and did the deletion have a polar effect on the adjacent yhoB & degQ genes?
2. The authors report using FPKM as input into edgeR for differential abundance analysis. This is incorrect, as edgeR’s TMM normalization method assumes that raw counts are input. As such, this analysis must be redone to properly assess differential abundance. Are the author reporting uncorrected or corrected p values (line 557)?
3. For the bacterial growth assay, only aerobic conditions are mentioned (line 561). Given the presentation of both aerobic/anaerobic growth assays, can the authors clarify this?
4. For the bacterial replication assay, the authors note that the cultures were shaken under aerobic conditions (line 568-9), but do not make this comment for the anaerobic conditions. Were the cultures grown statically under anaerobic conditions and would that impact the results?
5. The authors present growth data as both classical cell density measurements (eg. S5C S7AB) and also as log2(relative replication ratio). How is relative replication ratio calculated and why is this used instead of growth curves in the main manuscript but not the supplemental?
6. The use of nitrate by C. sakazakii appears to primarily occur under anaerobic conditions. The authors employ both aerobic and anaerobic culturing at various points in the manuscript and do not always clearly state or indicate on figures whether the growth was done aerobically/anaerobically (e.g. FigS2, Fig5E, Fig 6ACJK and others). This should be corrected.
7. What other transcripts would be predicted to be regulated by csrN in the same manner as narGHIJ based on binding to the 5’UTR?
8. The authors tested mutants in ΔnarGHJI, and ΔnarK for nitrate respiration, but didn’t appear to test the ΔcsrN mutant. Is the ΔcsnN mutant also impacted in nitrate respiration?
9. The authors tested the ΔcsnNΔnarGHJI in vivo, but do not appear to have tested the ΔcsnN mutant. Is the ΔcsrN mutant also impacted in vivo?
10. Related to above comments, the authors show that the CsrNmut is impacted in colonization. What validation experiments did the authors do to determine whether transcripts other than narGHIJ would be impacted by this mutation? Did the authors test a strain where both the csrN and narGHIJ 5’UTR were mutated to see if this restores function?
11. The authors suggest that tungsten supplementation in vivo impacts infection through nitrate metabolism as the WT strain showed reduced colonization whereas the ΔnarGHJI mutant appeared unaffected. The authors should demonstrate that tungsten does not impact in vitro growth of the WT & ΔnarGHJI strains (aerobically/aerobically) and that it also impacts nitrate utilization in the WT strain. Titrating with molybdenum (the presumed cofactor that tungsten is replacing) would also be a very useful mechanistic demonstration.
12. The model presented in figure 8 has several aspects that should be improved:
a. It seems to imply that C. sakazakii is a gram positive (single membrane layer between extracellular /cytoplasm space)
b. What is “inflammatory factor” in this model?
c. Why have nitrate represented by both a green dot and also write out NO3-?
d. The model should include the proposed mechanism whereby tungsten would inhibit this pathway
e. Explicitly incorporating host elements (e.g NOS via Nos2) into the model and its interaction with C. sakazakii would be useful.
13. Did the authors assess the impact of tungsten on their rat microbiomes? While previous report suggested that tungsten may have minimal impact on mouse microbiotas, this should be validated in this rat model.
14. On a similar line of thought, the authors tone down the statement that tungsten does not adversely affect the commensal microbiota (line 458), as a single paper is being referenced. This is likely an oversimplification as numerous bacteria employ molybdate cofactors for and would be susceptible to the same tungsten-mediated poisoning. Moreover, any therapies for targeting C. sakazakii would naturally be employed in infants who may be more susceptible to microbiota alterations given their young age.
15. Figure 5B shows an increase in nitrate production in RAW264.7 cell over time. Did the authors do a mock infection to determine if nitrate is being induced by infection vs accumulating over time?
16. The statement in lines 428-430 stating that “aerobic respiration” being dispensable for virulence is to broad. Only single deletion mutants were tested and there could be compensation between the pathways both in vivo and in vitro should the appropriate substrates be present.

### Reviewer 2

The authors reported a signal transduction pathway centered on a novel sRNA, CsrN, which facilitates C. sakazakii in utilizing nitrate respiration in response to oxygen-limited environments within the host, thereby enhancing its virulence in vivo. There were some major concerns need to be addressed.
1. Lines 21 and 54, C. sakazakii infections are usually associated with powdered infant formula, but the link with rice-based supplementary food remains contentious. The authors should provide sufficient references—specifically clinical case reports with supporting epidemiological data—to substantiate this assertion regarding rice-based products.
2. Line 145-150, It remains unclear whether the reported bacterial counts represent C. sakazakii exclusively or include other microorganisms. Please specify the selective/differential medium used for plating, as this critically impacts data interpretation. Figure 2C-D presents survival rates and bioluminescent imaging for wild-type and ΔCsrN. To establish genetic causality, data for the complemented strain (ΔCsrN+pCsrN) must be included. This control is essential to demonstrate that observed phenotypes result specifically from CsrN deletion rather than secondary mutations.
3. Beyond the CGG motif in hairpin loop of CsrN, whether other nucleotides within the complementary region between 5′ UTR of narGHJI mRNA and the CsrN sRNA affect their binding interaction?
4. To establish that CsrN increases the expression of narGHJI by influencing its mRNA stability, the authors should perform genetic complementation experiments using a CsrN-expressing plasmid in ΔCsrN strains.
5. Line 231-234, the survival of ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI exhibited no significant difference from that of ΔnarGHJI, the author speculated CsrN deletion did not affect the bacterial survival in macrophages in a ΔnarGHJI background. This experiment lacked the essential control group: the ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI strain complemented with CsrN (ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI + pCsrN).
6. The most significant limitation of this study is that, beyond comparing bacterial loads, it lacks supporting pathological evidence to substantiate the changes in C. sakazakii virulence following gene knockout. Crucially, data demonstrating differences in key indicators of pathogenicity – such as cytopathy, cytotoxicity/cell damage, inflammatory cytokine levels, and histopathology of affected organs – are missing. Furthermore, the ultimate cause of death in the infected mice remains undefined.
While the ΔnarGHJI mutant group showed approximately 20% survival at 96 hours, all mice infected with the wild-type (WT) strain and the other knockout mutants (including the ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI double mutant) succumbed to infection. The observed difference in time-to-death between WT-infected mice and knockout mutant-infected mice was only about 24 hours. This relatively short time difference raises questions about the magnitude and biological significance of the attenuation in virulence attributed to the gene knockouts.
Consequently, while the study effectively demonstrates that CsrN and narGHJI knockouts impact the total bacterial load in vivo, it lacks direct evidence linking these genetic modifications to a definitive change in C. sakazakii virulence.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript investigates a regulatory pathway in Cronobacter sakazakii that connects the global regulator ArcA, the small RNA CsrN, and the nitrate reductase operon narGHJI. RNA-seq identifies narGHJI as a CsrN-upregulated operon. The authors demonstrate that CsrN base pairs directly with the narG 5′UTR to stabilize its mRNA, and that ArcA binds to the csrN promoter to activate transcription. Evidence is provided from different models linking this regulatory cascade to survival and pathogenesis. Finally, they show that sodium tungstate, a nitrate reductase inhibitor, reduces bacterial burden and prolongs host survival. A noteworthy strength is that the phenotypes are clearly observed in a ΔcsrN strain. For many sRNAs, only overexpression reveals an effect, but here the loss-of-function phenotype is strong and reproducible. This underscores the biological importance of CsrN and strengthens the conclusions.
Overall, the study is conceptually appealing: it defines a regulatory chain from a global transcriptional regulator (ArcA), through an sRNA (CsrN), to a metabolic operon (narGHJI), establishing a direct link between regulatory RNA biology, metabolism, and virulence. Nevertheless, several comments and questions, listed below, could further improve the manuscript.
1. Persistence and infection strategy
The data clearly support bacterial persistence in host niches—specifically survival in macrophages and colonization of inflamed, oxygen-limited tissues—driven by nitrate respiration. The manuscript uses “persistence” in this ecological/pathophysiological sense. However, antibiotic persistence (tolerance to bactericidal drugs) is not addressed, even though nitrosative stress is known to shape persistence in enteric pathogens. Incorporating antibiotic-challenge assays in infected cells would broaden the impact and connect the findings to the antibiotic persistence field.
2. ΔarcA virulence phenotype
The ΔarcA strain is analyzed in depth for gene expression: ArcA binds the csrN promoter and is required for csrN and narGHJI induction under anaerobic conditions and during infection. While this firmly establishes transcriptional control, I did not see direct in vivo virulence data for ΔarcA (e.g., reduced colonization or systemic spread in the rat model). Including ΔarcA infection data with complementation would fully close the regulatory loop from sensor (ArcA) to virulence phenotype.
3. Role of Hfq
Since most sRNAs in enterobacteria require Hfq for stability and function, the role of Hfq in C. sakazakii deserves clarification. Does Hfq bind and stabilize CsrN as in other Enterobacteriaceae? If this has not been directly tested, a brief discussion of this point would help readers interpret the generalizability of the mechanism.
4. Conservation of CsrN
The manuscript shows that CsrN is conserved across C. sakazakii species. What about conservation in other Gram-negative bacteria? If CsrN or a homolog exists more broadly, that could expand the significance of the findings.
5. Pathogen lifestyle and infection model
Is C. sakazakii considered a true intracellular pathogen? Are macrophages its preferred niche in vivo, or is the intracellular stage primarily a transient step during dissemination? The transition in the text to macrophage assays is quite abrupt. A fuller justification of the macrophage model’s relevance would help contextualize the intracellular findings.
6. Choice of animal model
The rationale for using neonatal rats instead of mice is not fully explained. Is this a validated or preferential model for C. sakazakii infection? A short justification would help. In addition, the term “systemic infection” may be too strong for a gavage model where blood samples were not collected to quantify bacteremia. It would be clearer to describe dissemination based on colonization of distal organs.

In our RNA-seq result, we found that degQ and yhcB were down-regulated in ΔCsrN

disrupted this predicted regulatory interaction. Within the predicted base-pairing region,

abolished the CsrN-mediated regulation on yhcB. In contrast, the expression of

significant difference from that of WT strain (Response Fig. 1a). Moreover, we also
showed that there was no significant difference in bacterial burdens in small intestine,
colon, blood, liver and spleen between rats infected with CsrNmut-y or WT strain
(Response Fig. 1b). These data indicate that the CsrN-yhcB regulatory interaction does
not influence bacterial virulence.
Collectivelly, these data showed that the impaired survival in macrophages and
dissemination in the host observed in ΔCsrN are not due to the downregulation of degQ
or yhcB.

These results have been added in lines 341-352 of the revised manuscript.
Response Fig. 3 Replication of C. sakazakii WT, CsrN and narGHJI strains in M9 medium
under anaerobic conditions. Relative replication ratio was the fold change in growth at 1, 4, and 24
hours / 0 hours. n = 3 independent experiments.
9. The authors tested the ΔcsnNΔnarGHJI in vivo, but do not appear to have tested the
ΔcsnN mutant. Is the ΔcsrN mutant also impacted in vivo?
Response: Thank you for the comments. We have investigated the role of CsrN in
bacterial pathogenicity in vivo by orally infecting 2- to 5-day-old rats with WT, CsrN
and ΔCsrN complemented strains. The results showed that rats infected with CsrN
exhibited significantly decreasd bacterial burdens in the small intestine, colon, blood,
liver, and spleen compared to those infected with WT and ΔCsrN complemented strain,
suggesting that CsrN contributes to both GIT colonization and systemic dissemination
by C. sakazakii within the host (Fig. 2B). Additionally, we have tested the survival
curves of rats orally infected with WT, CsrN or ΔCsrN complemented strains. The
result showed that rats infected with CsrN exhibited prolonged survival times
compared to those infected with WT or ΔCsrN complemented strains (Fig. 2C).
Bioluminescence imaging (BLI) showed that rats infected with CsrN-Lux exhibited
significantly reduced systemic dissemination within the host compared with those
infected with WT-Lux (Fig. 2D). Moreover, we found that the levels of IL-6 and TNF-
α, as well as the histopathology scores, were significantly higher in WT-infected rats
than those infected with CsrN (Fig. 2E-F and Supplementary Fig. 2D). These results
suggest that CsrN plays a critical role in enhancing the virulence of C. sakazakii in vivo.
10. Related to above comments, the authors show that the CsrNmut is impacted in
colonization. What validation experiments did the authors do to determine whether
transcripts other than narGHJI would be impacted by this mutation? Did the authors
test a strain where both the csrN and narGHJI 5’UTR were mutated to see if this restores
function?
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. According to your suggestions,
we constructed a double mutant strain 5′ UTRmut-narCsrNmut by simultaneously mutating
the binding motif in 5′ UTR of narGHJI (CCG to GCU) and CsrN (CGG to AGC) on
the chromosome of WT. Then, we investigated whether this double mutation can restore
bacterial survival in macrophages and systemic dissemination in the host, compared to
the single mutation in CsrN (CsrNmut) or 5′ UTR of narGHJI (5′ UTRmut-nar). We
reperformed the infection assays using WT, CsrNmut, 5′ UTRmut-nar, and 5′ UTRmut-
narCsrNmut both in vitro and in vivo. The result showed that both 5′ UTRmut-nar and
CsrNmut strains exhibited significantly reduced survival in macrophage at 1, 4, 24 hpi
compared to WT or 5′ UTRmut-narCsrNmut strain, whereas there was no significant
difference in survival between 5′ UTRmut-narCsrNmut and WT in macrophages
(Supplementary Fig. 4H). Moreover, we also investigated whether double mutation
restored bacterial virulence in vivo. The results showed that 5′ UTRmut-nar and CsrNmut
strains exhibited markedly attenuated systemic dissemination in neonatal rats compared
to WT or 5′ UTRmut-narCsrNmut strain, whereas the bacterial burdens in the small
intestine, colon, blood, liver, and spleen of rats infected by 5′ UTRmut-narCsrNmut or WT
exhibited no significant difference (Supplementary Fig. 4I). These results suggest that
the double mutation restores bacterial virulence compared to the single mutation in
CsrN or narGHJI, confirming that the impaired survival of ΔCsrN in macrophages and
its reduced systemic dissemination within host were due to the decreased expression of
narGHJI, rather than other transcripts. We have added these results in lines 291-295 of
the revised manuscript.
11. The authors suggest that tungsten supplementation in vivo impacts infection through
nitrate metabolism as the WT strain showed reduced colonization whereas the
ΔnarGHJI mutant appeared unaffected. The authors should demonstrate that tungsten
does not impact in vitro growth of the WT & ΔnarGHJI strains (aerobically/aerobically)
and that it also impacts nitrate utilization in the WT strain. Titrating with molybdenum
(the presumed cofactor that tungsten is replacing) would also be a very useful
mechanistic demonstration.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this crucial point. We have performed the
following experiments to address these points, and these data have been incorporated
into the revised manuscript (lines 438-449).
No difference in growth was observed between WT or ΔnarGHJI strain under aerobic
conditions, regardless of the presence of tungstate or molybdate (Supplementary Fig.
7E). The addition of nitrate significantly promoted WT growth under anaerobic
conditions. However, this growth-promoting effect was markedly inhibited upon co-
supplementation with tungstate (Supplementary Fig. 7C). Notably, in the presence of
both nitrate and tungstate, the addition of increasing concentrations of molybdate
progressively restored anaerobic growth of the WT (Supplementary Fig. 7C). In
contrast, supplementation with nitrate, tungstate or molybdate had no significant effect
on the growth of ΔnarGHJI under anaerobic conditions (Supplementary Fig. 7D).
These results suggest that tungsten supplementation impacts the growth of C. sakazakii
under anaerobic conditions is medicated through its effect on bacterial nitrate
metabolism.
12. The model presented in figure 8 has several aspects that should be improved:
a. It seems to imply that C. sakazakii is a gram positive (single membrane layer between
extracellular /cytoplasm space)
b. What is “inflammatory factor” in this model?
c. Why have nitrate represented by both a green dot and also write out NO3-?
d. The model should include the proposed mechanism whereby tungsten would inhibit
this pathway
e. Explicitly incorporating host elements (e.g NOS via Nos2) into the model and its
interaction with C. sakazakii would be useful.
Response: Thank you for the comments. We have modified the Figure 8 according to
your suggestions. C. sakazakii is a Gram-negative bacteria, and we have showed the
double membrane layer between extracellular /cytoplasm space. The “inflammatory
factor” in the original Fig. 8 has been changed into inducible nitric oxide synthase
(iNOS) and its product, nitric oxide (NO). The representation of nitrate has been
standardized to its chemical formula (NO₃⁻). The tungsten inhibition pathway has been
included in the revised Figure 8.
13. Did the authors assess the impact of tungsten on their rat microbiomes? While
previous report suggested that tungsten may have minimal impact on mouse
microbiotas, this should be validated in this rat model.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. To investigate the effect of tungstate
treatment on the microbiota of neonatal rats, 2-day-old rats were treated with tungstate.
After two days, DNA extracted from the caecal content of tungstate-treated rats and
control rats was analysed by high-throughput gene-sequencing of 16S rRNA. By
analyzing the alpha diversity, we found that Chao index and Shannon index between
the tungstate group and mock group exhibited no significant difference (Supplementary
Fig. 7F). The result of principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) using Bray-Curtis metric
distances of beta diversity also showed that tungstate treatment did not significantly
alter the intestinal bacterial diversity (Supplementary Fig. 7G). Moreover, we assessed
the relative abundance of the gut microbiota in each group. Consistently, variations at
the genus level also showed that tungstate treatment did not alter the overall community
structure (Supplementary Fig. 7H-I). We have added these results and descriptions in
lines 455-462 of the revised manuscript.
14. On a similar line of thought, the authors tone down the statement that tungsten does
not adversely affect the commensal microbiota (line 458), as a single paper is being
referenced. This is likely an oversimplification as numerous bacteria employ
molybdate cofactors for and would be susceptible to the same tungsten-mediated
poisoning. Moreover, any therapies for targeting C. sakazakii would naturally be employed in
infants who may be more susceptible to microbiota alterations given their young age.
Response: Thank you for the comments. As your concern above, we performed 16S
rRNA sequencing on bacterial DNA from the caecal content of tungstate-treated and
control rats. The results showed that tungstate treatment did not significantly alter the
intestinal bacterial diversity and community structure of the gut microbiota
(Supplementary Fig. 7F-I). For details, please see the response to your Comment 13.
In addition, according to your comments, the sentence “Importantly, tungsten has been
shown not to adversely affect commensal microbiota” has been changed to “ In light
of both our work and prior evidence, tungsten appears to have a minimal effect on
commensal microbiota, though further validation is warranted” (line 524-526 of the
revised manuscript).
15. Figure 5B shows an increase in nitrate production in RAW264.7 cell over time. Did
the authors do a mock infection to determine if nitrate is being induced by infection vs
accumulating over time?
Response: Thank you for the comments. According to your suggestions, we
remeasured nitrate levels in the supernatant of infected and un-infected macrophage
cultures at 1, 4, 24 hpi to determine whether nitrate production is induced by infection
or accumulates over time. The results showed a slight time-dependent increase in nitrate
levels in uninfected macrophages; however, the nitrate levels were significantly higher
in macrophages infected with C. sakazakii at all time points. These data indicate that
infection of C. sakazakii induces the nitrate accumulation in macrophages. The relevant
result have been updated in Fig. 5B.
16. The statement in lines 428-430 stating that “aerobic respiration” being dispensable
for virulence is to broad. Only single deletion mutants were tested and there could be
compensation between the pathways both in vivo and in vitro should the appropriate
substrates be present.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. We have now rewritten the sentence “our
study found that aerobic respiration is dispensable for the virulence of C. sakazakii both
in vivo and in vitro (Figs. 7A-C)” into “our study found that deletion of the cydAB,
which encodes cytochrome bd oxidase, had no significant effect on the virulence of C.
sakazakii both in vivo and in vitro (Fig. 7A-C)” in lines 494-496 of the revised
manuscript.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors reported a signal transduction pathway centered on a novel sRNA, CsrN,
which facilitates C. sakazakii in utilizing nitrate respiration in response to oxygen-
limited environments within the host, thereby enhancing its virulence in vivo. There
were some major concerns need to be addressed.
1. Lines 21 and 54, C. sakazakii infections are usually associated with powdered infant
formula, but the link with rice-based supplementary food remains contentious. The
authors should provide sufficient references—specifically clinical case reports with
supporting epidemiological data—to substantiate this assertion regarding rice-based
products.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. According to the literature, C.
sakazakii has been isolated in infant supplementary food in both China and Brazil over
the past five years (Food Res Int. 2020;137:109643. Microbiol Spectr.
2022;10(5):e0119722). However, we did not find any reported clinical case attributed
specifically to rice-based supplementary food. Therefore, we revised the sentence to:
“Although C. sakazakii is ubiquitous in the environment, its primary transmission
source is reconstituted powdered infant formula (PIF)” in lines 51-53 of the revised
manuscript.
2. Line 145-150, It remains unclear whether the reported bacterial counts represent C.
sakazakii exclusively or include other microorganisms. Please specify the
selective/differential medium used for plating, as this critically impacts data
interpretation. Figure 2C-D presents survival rates and bioluminescent imaging for
wild-type and ΔCsrN. To establish genetic causality, data for the complemented strain
(ΔCsrN+pCsrN) must be included. This control is essential to demonstrate that
observed phenotypes result specifically from CsrN deletion rather than secondary
mutations.
Response: Thank you for the comments. The bacteria strain used in this study carry
different antibiotic resistance, for instance, the WT strain spontaneously developed
resistance to nalidixic acid; the mutant strains are resistant to chloramphenicol; and the
complementary strains carry resistance corresponding to the plasmid they harbored. We
determined the colony count of C. sakazakii by plating samples on antibiotic-containing
agar.
As suggested, we have now performed additional experiments and included the
complemented strains (ΔCsrN+pCsrN and ΔnarGHJI+pnarGHJI) in Fig. 2C-D and
4C-D. The results demonstrated that complementation with CsrN or narGHJI restored
the systemic dissemination defects observed in the ΔCsrN and ΔnarGHJI, as
demonstrated by in vivo bioluminescent imaging (Fig. 2D and 4D). Consistently, the
pathogenicity of the complemented strains were restored to WT levels, as reflected by
the survival curves of infected rats (Fig. 2C and 4C). These results have been
incorporated into Fig. 2C-D and 4C-D and lines 160-169, 268-272 of the revised
manuscript.
3. Beyond the CGG motif in hairpin loop of CsrN, whether other nucleotides within the
complementary region between 5′ UTR of narGHJI mRNA and the CsrN sRNA affect
their binding interaction?
Response: Thank you for the comments. In bacteria, RNA stem-loops contributes to
the initial recognition events between RNAs, often facilitating hairpin loop-loop and
loop-linear interactions (Nucleic Acids Res. 2010;38(10):3489-3501; Biochimie.
2002;84(9):925-944). Within the stem-loop structure of RNA molecule, the stem is
composed of base-paired nucleotide forming a stable double helix, whereas the loop is
an unpaired region that forms a characteristic hairpin-like structure (Nat Commun. 2021
May 5;12(1):2530). Compared to the stem structure, the loop often provides a more
flexible and accessible conformation for initiating molecular recognition, enabling
specific base-pairing interactions (Biochimie. 2002;84(9):925-944). In the case of CsrN,
the other nucleotides in CsrN which complemented with the 5′ UTR of narGHJI mRNA
largely formed the stem structure, making them less likely to be directly involved in
target recognition. To investigate this further, we performed the Lux reporter assay
using ΔCsrN narGHJI-lux strain complementated with either wild-type CsrN or
CsrNstem-mut (with CGGGACGGCAGCGC mutated to CGGGACAGCAGCGC, which
had a mutation in the stem region without disrupting the overall stem-loop structure).
The result showed that overexpression of CsrN or CsrNstem-mut in ΔCsrN narGHJI-lux
strain both significantly increased luminescence intensity (Response Fig. 4). It
indicates that the complementary region between the stem region in CsrN and 5′ UTR
of narGHJI mRNA is not essential for the direct recognition to the target. However, the
stem region itself may provide a structure scaffold that facilitates the binding of the
hairpin loop in CsrN to the 5′ UTR of narGHJI mRNA.
Response Fig. 4 Expression of the 5′ UTR of narGHJI-lux fusion when CsrN or CsrNstem-mut was
overexpressed as indicated. n = 3 independent experiments.
4. To establish that CsrN increases the expression of narGHJI by influencing its mRNA
stability, the authors should perform genetic complementation experiments using a
CsrN-expressing plasmid in ΔCsrN strains.
Response: Thank you for the comments. We have performed additional experiments
and included the complemented strain (ΔCsrN+pCsrN) in Fig. 3N and O.
5. Line 231-234, the survival of ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI exhibited no significant difference
from that of ΔnarGHJI, the author speculated CsrN deletion did not affect the bacterial
survival in macrophages in a ΔnarGHJI background. This experiment lacked the
essential control group: the ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI strain complemented with CsrN
(ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI + pCsrN).
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. According to your suggestions,
we have now infected macrophages with WT, ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI or ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI
complemented with CsrN (ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI + pCsrN) strain. We found that the
survival of ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI and ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI + pCsrN in macrophages exhibited
no significant difference, but both were significantly reduced compared to WT
(Supplementary Fig. 4C), suggesting that CsrN deletion did not affect the bacterial
survival in macrophages in a ΔnarGHJI background. Moreover, we also performed
disseminated infection assay in 2- to 5-day-old rat pups orally infected with WT,
ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI or ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI + pCsrN strains. The results showed that the
survival rates and the bacterial burdens in the small intestine, colon, liver, spleen, and
blood of rat pups infected with either ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI or ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI + pCsrN
were comparable, but both were significantly lower than those infected with WT
(Supplementary Fig. 4E-F). These results confirmed that CsrN deletion did not affect
the systemic dissemination within the host in a ΔnarGHJI background. The relevant
results were updated in Supplementary Fig. 4C, 4E-F and lines 249-253, 273-280 of the
revised manuscript.
6. The most significant limitation of this study is that, beyond comparing bacterial loads,
it lacks supporting pathological evidence to substantiate the changes in C. sakazakii
virulence following gene knockout. Crucially, data demonstrating differences in key
indicators of pathogenicity – such as cytopathy, cytotoxicity/cell damage, inflammatory
cytokine levels, and histopathology of affected organs – are missing. Furthermore, the
ultimate cause of death in the infected mice remains undefined.
While the ΔnarGHJI mutant group showed approximately 20% survival at 96 hours,
all mice infected with the wild-type (WT) strain and the other knockout mutants (including
the ΔCsrNΔnarGHJI double mutant) succumbed to infection. The observed difference
in time-to-death between WT-infected mice and knockout mutant-infected mice was
only about 24 hours. This relatively short time difference raises questions about the
magnitude and biological significance of the attenuation in virulence attributed to the
gene knockouts.
Consequently, while the study effectively demonstrates that CsrN and narGHJI
knockouts impact the total bacterial load in vivo, it lacks direct evidence linking these
genetic modifications to a definitive change in C. sakazakii virulence.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. As recommended, we have now
detected the cytotoxicity in C. sakazakii infected macrophages, measured the level of
inflammatory cytokines and performed histopathological analysis in intestinal tissues
of infected rats. We found that the ΔCsrN and ΔnarGHJI strains were significantly less
cytotoxic to macrophages compared to WT strain (Supplementary Fig. 2C and 4D).
Moreover, the levels of TNF-α and IL-6 in the intestinal tissues of ΔCsrN- or
ΔnarGHJI-infected rats were significantly lower than those observed in WT-infected
rats (Supplementary Fig. 2D and 4G). Histological examination revealed that intestinal
segments from WT-infected rats exhibited significantly higher histopathology scores
compared to those infected with ΔCsrN or ΔnarGHJI (Fig. 2E-F and 4E-F). These
results suggest that the regulation of narGHJI by CsrN promotes the survival of C.
sakazakii in macrophages and enhances the systemic dissemination of bacteria in vivo,
leading to increased disease intensity in the hosts. These results have been added in
lines 146-151, 169-175, 253-257, 280-283 of the revised manuscript.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript investigates a regulatory pathway in Cronobacter sakazakii that
connects the global regulator ArcA, the small RNA CsrN, and the nitrate reductase
operon narGHJI. RNA-seq identifies narGHJI as a CsrN-upregulated operon. The
authors demonstrate that CsrN base pairs directly with the narG 5′UTR to stabilize its
mRNA, and that ArcA binds to the csrN promoter to activate transcription. Evidence is
provided from different models linking this regulatory cascade to survival and
pathogenesis. Finally, they show that sodium tungstate, a nitrate reductase inhibitor,
reduces bacterial burden and prolongs host survival. A noteworthy strength is that the
phenotypes are clearly observed in a ΔcsrN strain. For many sRNAs, only
overexpression reveals an effect, but here the loss-of-function phenotype is strong and
reproducible. This underscores the biological importance of CsrN and strengthens the
conclusions.
Overall, the study is conceptually appealing: it defines a regulatory chain from a global
transcriptional regulator (ArcA), through an sRNA (CsrN), to a metabolic operon
(narGHJI), establishing a direct link between regulatory RNA biology, metabolism, and
virulence. Nevertheless, several comments and questions, listed below, could further
improve the manuscript.
1. Persistence and infection strategy
The data clearly support bacterial persistence in host niches—specifically survival in
macrophages and colonization of inflamed, oxygen-limited tissues—driven by nitrate
respiration. The manuscript uses “persistence” in this ecological/pathophysiological
sense. However, antibiotic persistence (tolerance to bactericidal drugs) is not addressed,
even though nitrosative stress is known to shape persistence in enteric pathogens.
Incorporating antibiotic-challenge assays in infected cells would broaden the impact
and connect the findings to the antibiotic persistence field.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. According to your suggestions,
we performed the C. sakazakii antibiotic survival assays in infected macrophages,
following a previously published protocol (Cell Host Microbe. 2023;31(6):993-
1006.e6). Briefly, RAW264.7 cells were infected with WT, ΔCsrN and ΔnarGHJI
strains grown to the logarithmic phase at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 100. After
45 minutes of incubation post-infection, a portion of the infected macrophages was used
to assess bacterial invasion prior to antibiotic treatment. Intracellular bacteria were
extracted by lysing the macrophages with 0.1 % Triton X-100 (Sigma), followed by
ten-fold serial dilutions in PBS and plating on LB agar to determine CFU counts at time
point T0. The remaining infected macrophages were treated with antibiotic by replacing
the medium with one supplemented with cefotaxime (100 μg/ml; TCI). At the indicated
time points, intracellular bacteria were again extracted as described above and plated
on LB agar to assess antibiotic survival. We found that the survival of ΔCsrN and
ΔnarGHJI showed no significant difference compared with the WT strain in
macrophages under antibiotic treatment (Response Fig. 5), suggesting that nitrate
respiration is dispensable for antibiotic persistence in C. sakazakii.
Response Fig. 5 Kinetics of cefotaxime survival of C. sakazakii WT, ΔCsrN or ΔnarGHJI strain
in RAW264.7 cells. All values normalized to values after 45 min internalization (T0). n = 3
independent experiments.
2. ΔarcA virulence phenotype
The ΔarcA strain is analyzed in depth for gene expression: ArcA binds the csrN
promoter and is required for csrN and narGHJI induction under anaerobic conditions
and during infection. While this firmly establishes transcriptional control, I did not see
direct in vivo virulence data for ΔarcA (e.g., reduced colonization or systemic spread
in the rat model). Including ΔarcA infection data with complementation would fully
close the regulatory loop from sensor (ArcA) to virulence phenotype.
Response: Thank you for the comments. According to your comments, we have now
infected macrophages with WT, ΔarcA or ΔarcA complemented strain. We found that
the survival of ΔarcA in macrophages was significantly lower than WT and ΔarcA
complemented strain (Supplementary Fig. 6M). Moreover, we also performed
disseminated infection assay in 2- to 5-day-old rat pups orally infected with WT, ΔarcA
or ΔarcA complemented strain. The results showed that at 48 hpi, the bacterial burdens
in the small intestine, colon, liver, spleen, and blood of rat pups infected with ΔarcA
were significantly lower than those in rats infected with WT or ΔarcA complemented
strain (Fig. 6J). These results suggest that ArcA, which activates the nitrate respiration
under anaerobic conditions, contributes to the virulence of C. sakazakii both in vitro
and in vivo. The relevant results have been included in Fig. 6J and Supplementary Fig.
6M and lines 405-408 of the revised manuscript.
3. Role of Hfq
Since most sRNAs in enterobacteria require Hfq for stability and function, the role of
Hfq in C. sakazakii deserves clarification. Does Hfq bind and stabilize CsrN as in other
Enterobacteriaceae? If this has not been directly tested, a brief discussion of this point
would help readers interpret the generalizability of the mechanism.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. In our study, we found that
deletion of hfq did not affect the expression and the stability of CsrN (Supplementary
Fig. 1B and 1C), indicating that CsrN functions in an Hfq-independent manner. This
finding is consistent with recent studies reporting a growing number of Hfq-
independent sRNAs in bacteria (Nature. 2023;618(7964):358-364; Mol Cells.
2019;42(5):426-439; J Bacteriol. 2006;188(2):576-586). To explore the distribution of
CsrN, we performed a homology search based on its nucleotide sequence. The results
showed that CsrN is only present in Cronobacter spp. These results suggest that CsrN
is a specific, Hfq-independent sRNA that contributes to the virulence of Cronobacter.
4. Conservation of CsrN
The manuscript shows that CsrN is conserved across C. sakazakii species. What about
conservation in other Gram-negative bacteria? If CsrN or a homolog exists more
broadly, that could expand the significance of the findings.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. As responsed above, we
performed a sequence homology search, which showed that CsrN is only present in
Cronobacter spp. We have added this result in lines 131-132 of the revised manuscript.
5. Pathogen lifestyle and infection model
Is C. sakazakii considered a true intracellular pathogen? Are macrophages its preferred
niche in vivo, or is the intracellular stage primarily a transient step during dissemination?
The transition in the text to macrophage assays is quite abrupt. A fuller justification of
the macrophage model’s relevance would help contextualize the intracellular findings.
Response: Thank you for the comments. C. sakazakii has not traditionally been
considered a true intracellular pathogen. However, it is worth noting that many bacteria
previously classified as extracellular, such as Escherichia coli, Group A Streptococcu,
Neisseria meningitides, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, have been shown to reside and
survive within host cells under certain conditions (Mol Microbiol. 2020;113(3):541-
545). Similarly, C. sakazakii has demonstrated a remarkable ability to survive inside
host macrophages (J Immunol. 2009 Nov 15;183(10):6588-99; Food Microbiol. 2021
Dec;100:103851). Importantly, intracellular survival within macrophages is an essential
step for C. sakazakii to establish systemic dissemination, as the pathogen can evade the
host immune defense, penetrate the tissue barrier, and translocate to the bloodstream,
liver, and spleen through macrophages (PNAS 2022;119(11):e2118002119; Microb
Pathog. 2022;169:105643; Microb Pathog. 2021;158:105064).
We have added this information in lines 66-69 of the revised manuscript.
6. Choice of animal model
The rationale for using neonatal rats instead of mice is not fully explained. Is this a
validated or preferential model for C. sakazakii infection? A short justification would
help. In addition, the term “systemic infection” may be too strong for a gavage model
where blood samples were not collected to quantify bacteremia. It would be clearer to
describe dissemination based on colonization of distal organs.
Response: Thank you for your important comments. The use of neonatal rats in our
study is based on well-established physiological and immunological differences
between rats and mice that make rats a more relevant model for neonatal systemic
infections, including those caused by E. coli K1, which is a pathogen with similar
invasive properties to C. sakazakii (Redox Biol. 2023;59:102588; Nat Commun.
2018;9(1):2296). As detailed in the referenced literature (J Vis Exp. 2014 Oct
29;(92):e52018), neonatal rats closely resemble human infants in their susceptibility to
systemic infection via the gastrointestinal route, displaying strong age-dependent
vulnerability. In contrast, mice are less suitable due to their rapid overwhelming by
systemic infection and lack of comparable age dependency. Importantly, α-defensins,
key antimicrobial peptides that protect against systemic invasion, are highly expressed
in Paneth cells and neutrophils in both humans and rats, but not in mice (J Vis Exp.
together with the neonatal rat’s established use in previous studies of C. sakazakii
pathogenesis, colonization, and systemic dissemination (e.g., J Infect Dis. 2008 Aug
15;198(4):586-93; mSystems. 2019 Aug 6;4(4):e00305-19.), makes it a validated and
preferential model for studying the virulence of C. sakazakii.
We agree that precision in terminology is crucial. In our results, as shown in the original
manuscript, we collected blood samples and quantified bacteremia (Fig. 2B, 4B, and
5G), which supports the use of "systemic infection" to describe the presence of
bacteria in the circulatory system. However, we acknowledge that the primary focus of
our analysis was on bacterial load in distal organs. Therefore, we have replaced the term
"systemic infection" with "systemic dissemination" throughout the revised manuscript.

## Paper

## Abstract

Cronobacter sakazakii is an important neonatal pathogen frequently associated with
powdered infant formula. However, the mechanisms by which C. sakazakii adapts to the host
environment and establishes systemic dissemination remain poorly understood. Here, we reveal a
signal transduction pathway centered on a novel sRNA, CsrN, which facilitates C. sakazakii in
utilizing nitrate respiration in response to oxygen-limited environments within the host, thereby
enhancing its virulence in vivo. C. sakazakii infection triggers an inflammatory response, leading
to the accumulation of host-derived nitrate, a key alternative electron acceptor. The expression of
CsrN is induced under anaerobic conditions via the ArcAB two-component regulation system.
CsrN subsequently enhances the expression of the narGHJI operon, which encodes a nitrate
reductase complex. This promotes the colonization of C. sakazakii in the gastrointestinal tract
and benefits its survival within macrophages, ultimately leading to increased systemic bacterial
dissemination and virulence in the host. We show that administration of tungstate, a specific
inhibitor of nitrate respiration, significantly attenuates C. sakazakii virulence in animal
experiments. This work provides novel insights into the survival and pathogenicity mechanisms
employed by C. sakazakii in host environments and suggests nitrate respiration as a potential
therapeutic target for combating C. sakazakii infections.

## Introduction

Cronobacter spp, are Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic bacteria recognized as
opportunistic pathogens that pose a serious threat to neonates and immunocompromised infants
1,2. Among them, Cronobacter sakazakii is the most clinically significant species, frequently
associated with both outbreaks and sporadic cases worldwide 3. Infection caused by C. sakazakii
can result in life-threatening conditions, such as bacteremia, sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis,
meningitis and brain abscesses, with reported mortality rate reaching up to 80% based on
epidemiological data 4,5. Survivors often suffer from long-term neurological complications,
including quadriplegia, hydrocephalus and delayed neural development 6. Although C. sakazakii
is ubiquitous in the environment, its primary transmission source is reconstituted powdered
infant formula (PIF) 7. This is largely attributed to the bacterium’s remarkable resistance to
desiccation, osmotic stress, and high temperature 1,2,6,8. Furthermore, the emergence of multi-
drug resistant C. sakazakii renders the effective treatment more challenging, which has been
regarded as an important concern in public health 9.

Beyond reducing contamination risks during PIF production, a comprehensive
understanding of the virulence mechanisms of C. sakazakii is essential for developing effective
preventive and therapeutic strategies. The infection process of C. sakazakii typically begins with
the colonization of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) 2. Several virulence factors contribute to the
ability of C. sakazakii to adhere to intestinal mucosal surfaces, among which OmpA and OmpX
play particularly prominent roles 7. Following colonization, C. sakazakii can translocate into the
bloodstream, where it exhibits systemic persistence by evading immune responses and
replicating within macrophages 7,10,11. Survival within macrophages is an essential step for C.
sakazakii to establish systemic dissemination, as the pathogen can evade the host immune
defense, penetrate the tissue barrier and translocate to the bloodstream, liver, and spleen through
macrophages 2,7,12. Furthermore, C. sakazakii is capable of penetrating the blood-brain barrier
(BBB) by invading human brain microvascular endothelial cells, ultimately leading to meningitis
7,13.

Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is essential for bacterial proliferation, serving as the primary
energy source for biosynthetic processes. Bacterial cells generate ATP through a series of redox
reactions, whereby electrons are transferred from electron donors, such as glucose, to electron
acceptors, with oxygen (O2) being the most efficient due to its high redox potential. This process
releases substantial free energy that fuels cellular activities 14. However, within host
environments, bacteria frequently encounters oxygen-limited conditions, which necessitate the
use of alternative electron acceptors, such as tetrathionate, nitrate and fumarate 15,16. The ability
to efficiently exploit these alternative respiratory pathways enable pathogens to maximize energy
production, thereby facilitating rapid proliferation and competitive advantage over commensal
microbes 14. However, the mechanisms by which C. sakazakii adapts to the gut environment and
establishes systemic dissemination remain largely unclear.

The process of C. sakazakii infection is shaped by a complex array of host environment
factors. In bacteria, small RNAs (sRNAs) play crucial roles in regulating gene expression in
response to changing environmental conditions 17. A critical regulatory mechanism employed by
many pathogens involves post-transcriptional modulation via sRNAs, which function by base-
pairing with specific mRNA targets to influence processes such as growth, metabolism, cell
signaling, and immune evasion 17-19. Despite their recognized importance in other bacterial
pathogens, the specific roles of sRNA in C. sakazakii virulence remain largely unexplored.

In this study, we identified a signal transduction pathway that activates nitrate respiration,
thereby enhancing the pathogenicity of C. sakazakii through an sRNA, CsrN. We found that the
expression of CsrN is induced by the ArcAB two-component systems under anaerobic condition.
CsrN increases the expression of narGHJI, which encodes the nitrate reductase, by directly
binding to the 5′ untranslated region (UTR) of narGHJI mRNA. Activation of nitrate respiration
significantly promotes the survival of C. sakazakii in both the gut lumen and macrophages,
ultimately facilitating its systemic dissemination within the host. Furthermore, administration of
tungsten to neonatal rats significantly attenuated gastrointestinal colonization and systemic
dissemination of C. sakazakii by inhibiting the molybdenum-cofactor-dependent nitrate
respiration pathway. Our results suggest that targeting nitrate respiration may represent a
promising therapeutic strategy for combating C. sakazakii infection.
